followups.title: Growth: capacity or housing and amenities?
followups.context: D05: Your C is tentative. One capacity governs growth only; B separates housing from happiness and empire-wide resource pressures. Numerical examples are proposals.
followups.question: Which growth system should we specify?

options.text: A — One Settlement Capacity (recommended): e.g. capacity 6 slows growth near population 6; housing/water/service investment raises it. One meter, but no independent happiness economy.
B — Separate housing and amenities: a well-housed city can still be unhappy, and a happy city can lack housing. Richer tall/wide and trade decisions; more meters, content and shortage rules.
C — Housing only, explicitly named Housing: preserve the clearest Civ VI growth constraint; defer amenities. Simple and expandable, but fewer happiness/trade pressures.

followups.basis: User submitted all sixteen follow-up answers as A on 2026-10-27.

followups.title: Building chains: closer Civ VI structure or compact roles?
followups.context: D09: Both designs can use your placed sites. B groups several tiered buildings under districts with maintenance and advanced power needs; C uses shorter Minecraft chains and selected operating requirements.
followups.question: What should a mature specialized site contain?

options.text: A — Compact roles (recommended): e.g. Works with basic Workshop, a processing branch, and an Assembly upgrade; SU for powered machines and a few material recipes. Clear jobs; less tier breadth.
B — Closer Civ VI families: several tiers per specialty, broader gold maintenance and advanced SU requirements. More long-term investment; more operating budgets and mandatory-looking steps.
C — Hybrid: two or three tiers per site, with one mutually exclusive branch. More choice than a linear ladder; added branching and replacement rules.

followups.basis: User submitted all sixteen follow-up answers as A on 2026-10-27.

followups.title: Civics: independent progress or milestone doctrines?
followups.context: D11: A full second tree supplies a separate strategic clock; a doctrine track can offer empire policies without another yield or long tree. Both can support upkeep and Builder/Trader policy choices.
followups.question: Which organization system should we design?

options.text: A — Milestone doctrines (recommended): a small set of empire policies unlocked by broad achievements, not science alone. Fewer meters; fewer ways to invest deliberately in faster doctrine progress.
B — Compact independent civics: e.g. 12–18 Minecraft-themed charters using a culture-like yield. Choose science versus organization investment; adds a yield, producers and another research screen.
C — Fuller Civ VI-like civic tree and policy slots: deepest political planning; largest content and AI burden, even without diplomatic victory.

followups.basis: User submitted all sixteen follow-up answers as A on 2026-10-27.

followups.title: Bankruptcy: how close should we copy Civ VI?
followups.context: D24: CivCraft has gold, unit upkeep and forced removal. It lacks a complete policy/amenity/shortage ecosystem. Civ VI also permits forced disbanding; choosing B does not inherently protect veterans.
followups.question: Which budget and insolvency behavior do you mean by B?

options.text: A — Civ VI-inspired budgets with agency (recommended): visible forecasts, doctrine maintenance reductions, a bounded warning/retirement window, then a deterministic fallback. Preserves choice; an intentional adaptation.

B — Closest practical Civ VI bankruptcy: maintenance policies and escalating shortage penalties, including forced unit losses. Familiar pressure; still punitive, and amenity penalties require an equivalent system.
C — Keep current shortage behavior but add forecasts and maintenance doctrines. Smallest implementation; recent valuable units can still disappear under the current removal order.

followups.basis: User submitted all sixteen follow-up answers as A on 2026-10-27.

followups.title: Industrial victory: retain or remove?
followups.context: D27: You lean toward removal. A complementary network can reward production, logistics and repair independently of science; if it mostly repeats End preparation, it should not be a separate victory.
followups.question: What should happen to Industrial victory in the next version?

options.text: A — Remove it for now: industry supports Conquest and End Expedition; Score is the deadline fallback. Clearest scope, but only two active victory races remain.

B — Prototype a distinct network victory (conditional recommendation): specialize, transport and sustain public deliveries under disruption. A different peaceful route; extra balance work and possible overlap with End.
C — Make it an optional experimental victory, disabled by default. Preserves a testbed; splits balance and testing between rulesets.

followups.basis: User submitted all sixteen follow-up answers as A on 2026-10-27.

followups.title: Healing: confirm the change from your earlier rule
followups.context: D23: Earlier you explicitly wanted passive healing only at home and healers abroad. Your new B allows ordinary recovery abroad as Civ VI does. This is a real revision, not merely a thematic choice.
followups.question: Which healing rule is now intended?

options.text: A — Use your latest B: ordinary rest heals abroad at lower territory-dependent rates; healers improve recovery. More forgiving expeditions, but support is less essential.
B — Retain your earlier H1: ordinary rest heals only in owned territory; healers can heal abroad. Strong logistics identity; unsupported expeditions cannot recover.
C — Neutral camps only: ordinary healing at home or established camps; healers work elsewhere. Additional strategic footholds, but more rules and targets.

followups.basis: User submitted all sixteen follow-up answers as A on 2026-10-27.

followups.title: Builders and Traders without excessive orders
followups.context: D04 and D16 select actual civilian units; D20 now selects Civ VI-like grouping. These pieces need useful decisions without recreating the unit clutter you dislike.
followups.question: How should routine civilian work be controlled?

options.text: A — Queued Builder tasks and autonomous repeating Trader routes (recommended): choose improvements and destinations; units execute movement. Strategic choices remain; automation must stop safely when threatened.
B — Mostly manual orders: direct each Builder move and periodically renew trade routes. Maximum control; more repeated interaction and AI work.
C — Strong automation: assign a city development priority and preferred trade partners. Lowest order load; fewer individual land-use choices.

followups.basis: User submitted all sixteen follow-up answers as A on 2026-10-27.

followups.title: Focus slots and placed sites: use one limit
followups.context: D01–03 select a few visible sites, limited city focuses and simple geographic bonuses. Counting sites and focuses separately would unnecessarily restrict development.
followups.question: How should specialization slots relate to map sites?

options.text: A — One slot equals one specialty site (recommended): basic buildings and improvements use no slot; growth opens a small additional allowance. One understandable limit; switching needs a redevelopment cost.
B — Fixed specialty allowance per city: one or two sites regardless of population. Strong permanent roles; growth adds fewer strategic options.
C — Focus slots are bonus assignments, not construction limits: sites remain buildable, selected focuses make them efficient. Flexible, but cities may still converge on building everything.

followups.basis: User submitted all sixteen follow-up answers as A on 2026-10-27.

followups.title: Settler population cost versus P1 prices
followups.context: D06 B adds population loss to the already more expensive P1 Settler. Capacity, Builder investment and growth can compound that penalty.
followups.question: How should we integrate population-consuming Settlers?

options.text: A — Charge one population, with a dedicated price/growth recalibration (recommended). Clear expansion trade-off; P1 Settler numbers become a starting test rather than a fixed final price.
B — Charge one population and initially retain exact P1 prices. Clean ablation; greater risk of slow or punitive expansion.
C — Compare both candidates before selecting a default. Better evidence; leaves the new opening specification provisional for longer.

followups.basis: User submitted all sixteen follow-up answers as A on 2026-10-27.

followups.title: Builder improvements versus limited raiding
followups.context: D04 adds improvements; D22 currently limits raiding to important sites and transport. If farms and mines are immune, Builder investments have different military exposure from Civ VI.
followups.question: Which improvements should be pillageable?

options.text: A — Specialty sites, routes and strategic-resource improvements (recommended): meaningful industrial and military targets, bounded repair burden; ordinary food tiles are protected.
B — All worked improvements as in broader Civ VI-style pillaging: more tactical targets and raider value; more repair work and snowball risk.
C — Only sites and routes: simplest military interface; individual mines and farms remain safe even when occupied.

followups.basis: User submitted all sixteen follow-up answers as A on 2026-10-27.

followups.title: Unit roster: define the middle ground
followups.context: D17 seeks Civ-like roles with fewer definitions; D18 upgrades and D19 one formation tier should prevent repeated recruitment from filling the map.
followups.question: Which roster scope should guide the next content proposal?

options.text: A — Core land roles plus compact navy (recommended): melee, ranged, mobile, anti-mobile and siege, with milestone upgrades and a small support roster. Clear counters; some roles need map-specific justification.
B — Same core plus a minimal late airship layer: one strike role and one defense answer. More late-game variety; adds range, basing and interception rules.
C — Consolidate the current roster first, then identify gaps through play. Lower redesign risk; may preserve weak role coverage longer.

followups.basis: User submitted all sixteen follow-up answers as A on 2026-10-27.

followups.title: Wonder roster: between a few and a Civ-sized ecosystem
followups.context: D10 asks for a middle ground. A fixed count alone cannot ensure distinct strategies, and wonders must not become mandatory victory prerequisites.
followups.question: What initial scale should the wonder proposal target?

options.text: A — About 12–16 distinct wonders across six Ages (recommended): several strategic roles and geography conditions; each needs a viable non-wonder alternative.
B — About 18–24: more contested build choices; substantially more unique effects and AI valuations.
C — First redesign the existing six, then add wonders only where a specific strategic gap remains. Tightest scope; fewer simultaneous wonder races.

followups.basis: User submitted all sixteen follow-up answers as A on 2026-10-27.

followups.title: SU: where is mechanical capacity shared?
followups.context: D38 uses Create Stress Units. SU measures capacity and impact, not a stored fuel. Real shafts transmit rotation; railways should not silently transmit torque.
followups.question: What should be the boundary of a CivCraft kinetic network?

options.text: A — Per-city SU pool (recommended): local generators supply local machines, with no shaft routing. Strong city identity and low complexity; explicitly abstracts physical connections.
B — Per connected Works-site network: share only through explicit mechanical links. More faithful placement and raiding; extra connection rules and path checks.
C — Per-city pool plus transportable fuel/materials: generation stays local; trade supports remote steam plants. Rich interdependence; more resource and route dependencies.

followups.basis: User submitted all sixteen follow-up answers as A on 2026-10-27.

followups.title: SU overload and machine operating choices
followups.context: Actual Create stops an overstressed network. A strategy-game adaptation could instead allocate capacity by player priority. Neither should subtract SU permanently each round.
followups.question: What should happen when machine impact exceeds capacity?

options.text: A — Player priority/activation list (recommended): lower-priority powered operations pause; basics continue. Readable choices, but deliberately differs from full-network Create stalling.
B — Create-like network stall: all kinetic machinery on that network stops until capacity or load is corrected. Faithful and consequential; a raid or new machine can cause a sharp cascade.
C — Block voluntary overloading, but stall after damage: construction warns or requires spare capacity; raids can still interrupt the network. Fewer accidental mistakes; extra exception rules.

followups.basis: User submitted all sixteen follow-up answers as A on 2026-10-27.

followups.title: 250 turns: deadline or intended finish?
followups.context: D33 proposes 250 rather than 180 rounds. Increasing a deadline alone does not slow research, alter travel time or ensure eras are worth playing.
followups.question: What pacing target should simulations and playtests use?

options.text: A — 250-round deadline, most competitive wins targeted around rounds 180–230 (recommended starting hypothesis). Room for recovery and contests; requires retiming and measured playtests.
B — A typical game should last around 250 rounds, with a later deadline. Longer strategic arc; more human and ComputerCraft turn workload.
C — Offer 180-round Quick and 250-round Standard, calibrated separately. More player choice; larger test matrix and separate travel/economy tuning.

followups.basis: User submitted all sixteen follow-up answers as A on 2026-10-27.

followups.title: Resource scarcity and viable strategies
followups.context: D15 selects Civ VI-like stockpiles and consumption, with Minecraft materials. Upgrades, SU fuel and trade can amplify bad resource starts; viability across factions needs alternative access.
followups.question: How should a player without a key local resource remain competitive?

options.text: A — Costly access alternatives (recommended): imports, village contracts and selected inferior substitutes. Scarcity matters without hard exclusion; fallback prices need testing.
B — Hard local/import dependence: fight, settle or negotiate for the resource. Strong geography and diplomacy; particular starts or hostile opponents can shut out a unit family.
C — Guarantee access to essential early inputs near every start; scarce advanced resources remain contested. Fairer openings; less early geographic asymmetry.

followups.basis: User submitted all sixteen follow-up answers as A on 2026-10-27.
